Both Sinclair and Hall led the race’s opening climb, and Sinclair was alone at the front for all of the race’s final three-quarters. Hall traded the women’s lead with challenger Antonina Iushina (Neutral) near halfway, but also essentially led all of the race.
Ultra-Trail Cape Town was the final contest of this year’s World Trail Majors and the year’s last major international ultramarathon. The race was part of a six-day event featuring six races ranging from 16 kilometers to 100 miles.
The 99k (61.5 miles) course is a real mountain run with 4,676 meters (15,341 feet) of climbing. It’s technical, steep, and the elevation gain is very front-loaded. The course’s high point at Platteklip Gorge is at about 25k (15.5 miles) into the race and comes after a 900-meter (3,000 feet) climb that’s sometimes steeper than 35 degrees. After that early climb, the race heads back to sea level. The final 55k (34 miles) has four smaller but still significant climbs before finishing back in Cape Town.
Two-time winner and 2025 runner-up Dmitry Mityaev (Neutral) was counted on as one of the men’s favorites. Mityaev’s 2022 win was a first-place tie with Hannes Namberger (Germany), who was also competing this year. Caleb Olson (U.S.), the 2025 Western States 100 winner and 2026 UTMB third-place finisher, was among the pre-race favorites too. None could come close to matching Sinclair on this day, though.

Forrest Gump has nothing on Cameron Balser.
Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S. in record time.
Averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m. PT on October 10 and ran across parts of 11 states before crossing the George Washington Bridge and entering New York City at 11:02 p.m. ET on Friday night. After running a few brisk miles through Manhattan, he eventually met up with his mom, stepdad, and two sisters and slowed to a walk on the final few blocks on the way to his finishing point.
His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of New York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.
The only trouble was that when Balser arrived in Lower Manhattan with a gaggle of two dozen or so friends, family members, and random followers, they found all of the gates to City Hall Park closed and locked. So instead, he walked to a point adjacent to City Hall and, like Gump mythically did in Monument Valley, Utah, he just stopped.
Balser officially ended his relentless push across the country at 11:45 p.m., which means he covered the 3,067-mile journey in a record-breaking 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes—roughly 13 hours and 45 minutes faster than Kostelnick.
“I know it was about the record, but mainly it was about us coming together and being together and loving one another,” Balser told the group around him after he finished. “We shared this experience, and I am so lucky and grateful to be able to do this, and I couldn’t have done it without so many people. I am grateful for this life and I’m going to keep living it like I do. So thank you so much, it means so much to me to have your support.”
Shortly thereafter, his crew and family members celebrated with some late-night New York pizza and, after devouring a slice or two, Balser almost immediately crashed into a deep sleep.
“And we didn’t set an alarm for 5 a.m.,” crew chief Sam Yeary said.
Years in the Making
Balser caught the running bug in high school and continued running competitively as a middle-distance runner for Vincennes University. He went through some hard times in his early 20s and dealt with depression that took him to a dark place that had him pondering suicide. But with support from friends, a job as wellness and housekeeping director at the YMCA of Grant County in Marion, Indiana, and an immersion into ultrarunning races from 50K to 100 miles, Balser got a new lease on life and has been spreading joy ever since.

On Thursday, November 19, 2026, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction) posted its 2026 Sustainability Report and said it is rethinking the 2030 deadline for its net-zero goal. Its 2025 net emissions rose to 11.8 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, up 45% from 2024.
The stock closed Friday, November 20, at $560.84, down 5.93%. That drop came during a broad tech selloff. Shares fell 11.6% over the past week, then traded at $569.32 after hours.
If you own the stock, what the report measures matters more than the climate headline, because Meta wrote it and it is one of the few direct measurements of how physical the AI expansion has become.
What Meta Committed To
Meta set the goal in 2020: net zero across its whole value chain, plus water positive, by 2030. The report opens with a letter. In it, Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that Meta is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.”
They said AI demand grew faster than almost anyone projected, and clean energy fell behind because of years-long grid interconnection waiting lines, slow permitting, and lagging transmission. Meta says its long-term dreams are unchanged, but it gave no date for a revised plan.
How Emissions Jumped 45% on 100% Clean Power
Meta says it matched 100% of its electricity with clean and renewable energy for the sixth straight year. Direct Scope 1 emissions were just 33,555 tons, and market-based Scope 2 (purchased power) was 10,861 tons.
Almost all of the footprint is Scope 3, the emissions in Meta’s supply chain. Scope 3 amounted to 11,858,913 tons, about 99% of the total. Capital goods such as servers, chips, networking gear, steel and concrete made up 73%, and clean power contracts do little to reduce them.
Emissions Double as a Capex Gauge
Capital goods emissions rise with physical construction, so this footprint tracks spending. By our calculation, electricity use rose 34.9% to 24,849,122 megawatt-hours, and data centers used 24,523,035 of that. All of that steel, concrete, and power has to come from somebody, and we profiled seven of the suppliers behind the AI expansion in a free report.
Third-quarter capex was $34.906 billion[1], up 85.38%, and free cash flow was -$2.120 billion. Meta still guides 2026 capex to $135 billion to $145 billion[1].
That puts Meta’s interim Scope 3 target out of reach. By our math, 2025 Scope 3 was about 2.05 times the 5,772,583-ton 2021 baseline Meta aims not to exceed by end-2031. Reaching it would require cleaner suppliers or slower building.
Power Limits Threaten the AI Plan Itself
The interconnection waiting lines and permitting delays that slowed clean energy also limit how fast new data centers can come online. Mark Zuckerberg spoke on the October 21, 2026[2] earnings call. He said Muse is “very compute-intensive to run”[2] and that “we have not launched it globally yet.”
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL), Google’s parent company, faces the same pressure. It pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, stopped saying carbon-neutral operations by 2024, and has acknowledged that its emissions are still rising.

On a late November day on the U.S. East Coast, Americans Sydney Welch and Coleman Cragun took home wins in the JFK 50 Mile, one of the oldest and most historic ultramarathons in the U.S. Cragun gained some separation after the initial Appalachian Trail section and held off several fast runners in the flatter final 35 miles to finish in 5:29:13, while Welch put in an incredibly impressive performance to finish in 6:04:03, the second-fastest time in race history.
Several hours earlier, at 6:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on Saturday, November 21, Cragun and Welch toed the start line in Boonsboro, Maryland, with 1,122 other runners to begin their 50-mile journey to Williamsport. Now in its 64th edition, the race attracts some of the top distance runners — ultrarunners, road marathoners, and everyone in between — hunting a fast 50-mile time on a storied course. The weather was typical of late fall on the East Coast — cloudy, with temperatures in the 40s Fahrenheit — perfect for fast racing.
The course starts with a 2.5-mile paved section before connecting with the Appalachian Trail and climbs nearly 1,200 feet in the first 5.3 miles, accounting for most of the course’s elevation gain. The 13-mile trail section is famously rocky and rooty, suiting runners with more trail experience, and then drops more than 1,000 feet in the last two miles of trail. At mile 15.5, runners exit the trail and end up on the C&O Canal Towpath, a fast and flat 26.3-mile section of gravel and dirt where runners can really start to move. Spectators and commentators alike like to analyze splits on this section, as it’s nearly equivalent to a marathon time. For the last eight-plus miles, runners traverse rolling country roads to the finish in Williamsport. It is, for these reasons, one of the true road-to-trail (or trail-to-road) races on the ultra calendar.
The race, which brings together elite and everyday runners, is steeped in American history. Inspired by former President Theodore Roosevelt, who, during his presidency in the early 1900s, required his military officers to cover 50 miles on foot in 20 hours, former President John F. Kennedy established a series of 50-mile races across the country for his own officers and any civilians seeking an endurance challenge. The first edition of the JFK 50 Mile took place in 1963, and it is now the only race from Kennedy’s original series that is still held every year. With the most prestigious award, the Kennedy Cup, awarded to the fastest military team, the race retains and celebrates its strong military roots.
2026 JFK 50 Mile Women’s Race
With none of last year’s top five returning, the race to be the women’s champion was wide open. Canada’s Maïka Lamoureux, sixth last year, was the top returner, while Courtney Olsen, the American 100k record holder and current 100k world champion, was making her JFK debut. Stephanie Bruce, who has three U.S. road running titles to her name, two in the 10k and another in the half marathon, was also expected to contend. A strong mix of more trail-focused runners, including Americans Sydney Welch and Tay Cavett and Canadian Élisa Morin, made it a compelling and hard-to-predict race.

Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she says. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. When temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.
But what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?
A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.
The good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.
How Cold Does It Have to Be to Affect Performance?
There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.
Temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he says.
Each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how quickly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.

Taking that rollover could cost her more than $30,000. Her shares carry an illustrative cost basis of $70,000, which leaves $350,000 of gain that built up inside the plan. If she rolls the shares into an IRA, every dollar of that gain will be taxed as ordinary income when she withdraws it.
One Rollover Form Erases Her Capital Gains Rate
IRS Publication 575 shows how this works. In its example, a plan participant sells stock distributed from his plan and rolls the $60,000 of proceeds into an IRA, and “the entire $60,000 rolled over will be ordinary income when he withdraws it from his IRA.”
She has another option. Under 26 U.S.C. § 402(e)(4)(B)[1], net unrealized appreciation (NUA) in employer shares received as part of a lump-sum distribution is left out of her gross income. She pays ordinary income tax on the basis now. The appreciation is taxed later at capital gains rates, when she sells.
A poster on the Bogleheads forum who was considering the same move laid out the steps. Open a taxable brokerage account and a rollover IRA, then ask the 401(k) custodian for a lump-sum distribution. The shares go to the brokerage account and everything else goes to the IRA.

Assume her IRA withdrawals land in the 24% bracket. For single filers in 2026, that bracket covers taxable income from $105,700 to $201,775.
Taking the full stock value out of an IRA at that rate costs about $100,800 in federal tax.
Under NUA, she owes 24% on the basis now, which is $16,800. When she sells, the gain is taxed at 15%. Single filers stay at that rate until taxable income tops $545,500.
That’s a $31,500 difference. It increases if her IRA withdrawals end up taxed above 24%.

Check Point Software Technologies NASDAQ: CHKP expects product revenue to return to growth in the second quarter of 2027 as it works through a sales force restructuring and prepares for another appliance refresh cycle, Global Head of Investor Relations Kip Meintzer said at a Stephens fireside chat.
Meintzer said product revenue is expected to remain slightly negative in the fourth quarter of 2026 and be less negative in the first quarter of 2027 before turning positive. The company also expects to introduce new appliances in late 2027 or early 2028, potentially starting another significant customer refresh cycle.
“Our support updates and maintenance and subscription have done well,” Meintzer said, adding that weaker product sales had also affected those revenue lines by reducing subscription overlap and appliance-related services.
Sales Changes and Delayed Refreshes
Meintzer said Check Point restructured its sales force to pursue more large new customers. More than 40% of sales representatives changed accounts, creating disruption and inaccurate sales data that affected the company’s forecasts, he said.
Some appliance refresh opportunities slipped into the following year, while new customer opportunities remained in play but take time to close. Meintzer said several large refresh deals had moved into the fourth quarter or 2027.
He reiterated the company’s view that the third quarter was the trough across most revenue lines, citing improved confidence in sales force projections. The expected fourth-quarter product revenue increase of approximately 49% from the third quarter reflects a combination of delayed deals, seasonal demand and timing, he said.
Check Point is also continuing to hire salespeople. Meintzer said the company now expects to complete its planned hiring of 300 people, representing a net increase of 150, during the first quarter rather than by year-end. Winning a large new customer typically takes 12 to 18 months, he said.
Subscriptions and AI Products
Discussing Check Point’s outlook for 2027 security subscription revenue, Meintzer characterized the company’s expectation as being in the vicinity of $1.5 billion, rather than necessarily exceeding that amount.
He said renewals could benefit as customers move from older, lower-priced three-year contracts to newer pricing. Check Point raised prices by 10% in July 2025 and implemented a further increase of 12% to 20% on Oct. 4. The subscription outlook assumes realizing an increase of roughly 4% to 6%, he said.
Meintzer also identified the AI Defense Plane as a potential contributor. The subscription provides functionality associated with Check Point’s AI Network Firewall and is the company’s highest-priced subscription, he said. He added that the financial impact of the firewall product remains to be seen.
In email security, Meintzer said revenue is reaching $250 million and that he sees no slowdown in the business. He also described secure access service edge, or SASE, as a potential “dark horse” for 2027, noting that Check Point completed its first seven-figure deal for the product in the previous quarter, covering more than 80,000 users.
Profitability and Growth Goals
Meintzer said Check Point is not pursuing growth at any price, but its near-term goal is to reach mid- to high-single-digit growth before advancing toward its longer-term double-digit aspiration. He said the company needs a clearer revenue outlook before providing a more precise margin framework.
